title: Homo sapiens
objectives: Identify anatomical features commonly used in recognising Homo sapiens.
Relate fossil and genetic evidence to African origins and dispersal.
Interpret cultural evidence without treating it as a simple species test.

glossary.definition: Still living, rather than extinct.
Use of objects or actions to represent meanings beyond their immediate physical function.
Different characteristics changing at different rates or in different combinations.

slides.title: Our species among the hominins
slides.html: All living humans belong to Homo sapiens, the only surviving species of the genus Homo. This shared membership does not mean that people are genetically or anatomically identical. Variation occurs within and between populations, and much variation overlaps. Modern populations must not be arranged as stages on a ladder from ancient to more evolved humans.

slides.title: Recognising the cranial pattern
slides.html: Comparisons often emphasise a relatively high, rounded cranial vault, reduced brow prominence, a less projecting face and a prominent bony chin. Early fossils can show mixtures of features rather than every typical modern trait together. Identification depends on the overall anatomy and context; one characteristic does not define every individual without exception.

diagram.caption: Schematic comparison landmarks, not a portrait or species diagnosis from one trait.

slides.title: An African origin with a long history
slides.html: Fossil evidence places early Homo sapiens in Africa by about 300,000 years ago. This updates older textbook accounts limited to roughly 200,000 years. Origins involved populations and changes through time, not necessarily a single sudden event at one small site. The oldest recognised fossil occurrence also remains dependent on discovery, dating and taxonomic interpretation.

slides.title: Dispersal and population contact
slides.html: Homo sapiens populations dispersed beyond Africa in more than one episode and interacted with other human lineages. Fossils, artefacts and genomic patterns constrain these histories, but no single find maps every route. Later migrations and gene flow also complicate modern distributions. Present-day location cannot simply be read as an unchanged record of the first arrival.

slides.title: Technology is evidence, not an identity badge
slides.html: Many sapiens populations used diverse stone, bone and other technologies. Blades, composite implements and carefully made small tools can reveal skilled production and particular activities. These features were not present everywhere at the same instant, and some were shared with other lineages. A species label should not be assigned solely from one tool form.

diagram.caption: Schematic flake and blade forms. Tool shape is cultural and functional evidence, not an exclusive biological-species marker.

slides.title: Symbols and archaeological context
slides.html: Pigments, ornaments, engravings and deliberately arranged objects can provide evidence relevant to symbolic behaviour. Their interpretation depends on context and alternative uses. Pigment may have practical as well as symbolic functions, and an ornament’s particular meaning may be unknown. State the observed material evidence before inferring communication, shared conventions or social identity.

slides.title: Bodies and behaviour vary
slides.html: Modern human body form reflects ancestry, development, environment and individual variation. Neither a particular body shape nor an artefact provides a simple measure of worth or intelligence. Fossil anatomy can illuminate functional constraints, while archaeology informs behaviour. These evidence types should be combined without assuming that every anatomical difference determines a fixed cultural difference.

slides.title: Biological and cultural change
slides.html: Biological evolution changes inherited population characteristics over generations. Cultural change spreads learned practices through teaching, imitation and communication, including between unrelated people. The two processes can influence one another, but they are not interchangeable. Changes in subsistence, settlement or technology can alter selection pressures without requiring every cultural innovation to originate as a new mutation.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes living humans?
options: Different modern populations represent successive ancient species.
Only some living populations belong to Homo sapiens.
All living humans belong to the same species, despite substantial variation.
Every member has identical anatomy and DNA.
feedback: Living populations are not stages on a fossil ladder.
The species includes all living human populations.
Correct. Shared species membership coexists with variation.
Variation occurs within a species.
questions.explanation: Correct. Shared species membership coexists with variation.

questions.prompt: Why should early Homo sapiens fossils be assessed using a suite of traits?
options: Different features can appear in different combinations during mosaic evolution.
The oldest fossil always has all modern traits.
A single tool always gives a species name.
Anatomical observations are never useful.
feedback: Correct. Early fossils may not display every typical modern feature together.
Early anatomy may contain a mixture of features.
Tools are not an exclusive species identity badge.
Anatomy remains central when interpreted with context.
questions.explanation: Correct. Early fossils may not display every typical modern feature together.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is justified by an engraved object in a securely dated context?
options: Its maker’s exact spoken sentence is recovered.
Every contemporary population used the same symbols.
It alone proves the maker’s entire genome.
It can contribute to an argument about symbolic behaviour, with context and alternatives considered.
feedback: An engraving does not preserve an exact spoken utterance.
One site cannot establish universal cultural practice.
Material culture is not a genome sequence.
Correct. Interpretation should remain tied to the evidence.
questions.explanation: Correct. Interpretation should remain tied to the evidence.

questions.prompt: How can a cultural practice spread without a new mutation?
options: It must first become a chromosome.
People can learn it from others, including unrelated individuals.
Every innovation requires a new allele in every participant.
Cultural transmission is impossible between populations.
feedback: A learned practice is not physically a chromosome.
Correct. Social learning transmits cultural information.
Learning does not require a new mutation in each learner.
Contact can transmit cultural practices across population boundaries.
questions.explanation: Correct. Social learning transmits cultural information.

questions.prompt: Explain why the phrase “modern humans evolved in Africa” is compatible with later admixture outside Africa.
questions.model: An African origin describes the evolutionary emergence of the lineage, while admixture describes later genetic exchange with other populations. A lineage can originate in one region, disperse and then interbreed elsewhere. Fossils and genomic evidence therefore address related but different events. This model does not require complete genetic replacement of every earlier population, nor independent origins of living human species in separate regions.
criteria: Separate origin from later contact.
Describe dispersal followed by interbreeding.
Avoid equating African origin with strict zero-admixture replacement.

questions.prompt: Describe how evidence for symbolic behaviour differs from direct knowledge of an ancient belief.
questions.model: An engraved object, ornament or deliberate arrangement may indicate shared representation or communication when its context supports that interpretation. The material can survive while its particular meaning is lost. Archaeologists must also consider practical uses and depositional processes. Consequently, evidence can support a general inference of symbolic activity without revealing the exact story, belief or spoken language of the people involved.
criteria: Give relevant material evidence.
Consider context or alternative practical uses.
Distinguish general symbolic inference from a specific recovered meaning.

summary: All living humans are Homo sapiens, not stages on an evolutionary ladder.
Early African sapiens evidence reaches about 300,000 years ago.
Anatomical suites and context support identification.
Learned cultural change and inherited biological evolution are distinct but interacting.
sourceNotes: Scope adapted from Surfing WACE Human Biology Unit 4 (2017); explanations, models and questions are original.
African fossil age and extant species context: https://humanorigins.si.edu/evidence/human-fossils/species/homo-sapiens
Exact ancient migrations and universal cultural thresholds are deliberately not asserted.

title: Dating Hominin Fossils
objectives: Choose dating methods appropriate to the material and question.
Interpret stratigraphic brackets and radioactive half-lives.
Distinguish age evidence from dietary, mobility and climate proxies.

glossary.definition: Study of the order and relationships of layers.
Adjustment against independent reference information to improve an estimate.
Time required for half the parent radioactive atoms in a closed population to decay.

slides.title: The dated event must be identified
slides.html: A reported age is meaningful only when the dated material and event are clear. A bone’s organic component, a volcanic crystal and sediment deposition can record different events. Dating an associated layer is not identical to directly dating a fossil. Context connects the measurement to the archaeological question, and the connection itself must be justified.

slides.title: Relative ordering from layers
slides.html: In an undisturbed sequence, lower deposited layers are older than those above. This relative ordering can place a fossil before or after another event without supplying a calendar age. Faulting, folding, erosion or redeposition can disturb a simple sequence. A fossil moved from an older layer may be older than the sediment currently surrounding it.

diagram.caption: A schematic undisturbed sequence. Ages for suitable volcanic material may bracket deposition of the fossil-bearing layer.

slides.title: Comparative fluorine evidence
slides.html: Buried bone can acquire fluorine from groundwater. Comparing bones exposed to sufficiently similar local conditions may help assess relative age or whether they share a burial history. Uptake also depends on groundwater and bone properties. Fluorine content is therefore not a universal clock that converts any bone concentration directly into a numerical age.

slides.title: Radioactive decay and elapsed time
slides.html: Radioactive parent atoms decay at a characteristic probability. After one half-life, half the original parent population remains; after two, one quarter remains. The fraction follows repeated halving, not subtraction of the same number each interval. Applying this relationship requires an appropriate system and an account of initial conditions and later gain or loss.

diagram.caption: Ideal closed-system decay: parent fractions after successive half-lives are 1, 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and 1/16.

slides.title: When radiocarbon is appropriate
slides.html: Radiocarbon dating measures the changing abundance of carbon-14 in suitable carbon-containing material after exchange with the environment ceases. Its half-life is approximately 5730 years. Useful dates generally extend to around 50,000 years, depending on sample and laboratory conditions. Contamination can distort results; calibration accounts for past variation in atmospheric carbon-14 rather than assuming a perfectly fixed initial ratio.

slides.title: Volcanic rocks and older contexts
slides.html: Potassium–argon and related argon methods can date suitable volcanic minerals, commonly providing ages for layers associated with much older hominin remains. They normally date mineral-system events rather than directly measuring the age of a fossil bone. The interpretation requires geological context and assessment of whether the isotopic system retained the relevant products after formation.

slides.title: Fission tracks and other clocks
slides.html: Spontaneous fission can leave damage tracks in suitable minerals or glass. Track accumulation and retention provide time-related information, but heating can affect the record. Different methods have different materials, ranges and assumptions. A long list of techniques does not mean that any technique can be applied to every specimen with equal reliability.

slides.title: Stable isotopes answer other questions
slides.html: Stable carbon or nitrogen isotope ratios can inform reconstructions of diet, while strontium and oxygen comparisons may help investigate origins or movement. These analyses usually require environmental reference values and physiological context. They are not automatically clocks. A dietary inference or a difference from local isotope values should not be reported as a direct numerical fossil age.

slides.title: Climate records provide context
slides.html: Ice cores, sediments and other environmental archives help reconstruct past climate. Their independently developed chronologies allow comparison with occupation and migration evidence. Correlation can suggest environmental pressures or opportunities but does not alone prove a particular cause of migration. Lower sea levels can expose land in some regions without creating a land bridge across every sea.

slides.title: Combining results with uncertainty
slides.html: A strong age argument uses stratigraphy, appropriate numerical methods and explicit uncertainty together. For example, a fossil-bearing layer between hypothetical volcanic dates of 1.8 Ma below and 1.6 Ma above is bracketed by those events if the sequence is secure. It is not necessarily exactly 1.7 Ma, and averaging the bounds cannot replace an independent measurement.

questions.prompt: A fossil lies between undisturbed ash layers dated 1.8 Ma below and 1.6 Ma above. What follows?
options: The fossil must be exactly 1.7 Ma.
The depositional context is bracketed by those dated events, subject to association assumptions.
The fossil is younger than both layers.
The ash directly measures the fossil’s birth date.
feedback: The midpoint is not a measured fossil age.
Correct. Stratigraphic order and dated events constrain the context.
The fossil-bearing layer is between, not above, both layers.
Mineral dating records a geological event, linked to the fossil through context.
questions.explanation: Correct. Stratigraphic order and dated events constrain the context.

questions.prompt: In an ideal closed sample, 12.5% of a parent isotope remains. How many half-lives have elapsed?
questions.explanation: 12.5% = 0.125 = 1/8 = (1/2)^3, so 3 half-lives have elapsed.

questions.prompt: Which proposed use of radiocarbon is most appropriate?
options: Direct dating of every million-year-old mineral
Dating a stone’s shape without carbon
Dating suitable late-Pleistocene organic remains with contamination controls
Replacing all stratigraphic observations
feedback: Radiocarbon is not the appropriate clock for all ancient minerals.
A shape alone supplies no carbon-14 measurement.
Correct. Material, age range and sample quality must suit the method.
Numerical dates still require context.
questions.explanation: Correct. Material, age range and sample quality must suit the method.

questions.prompt: What can a difference in tooth strontium isotope ratios from a local baseline suggest?
options: An automatically exact calendar age
A complete spoken language
The absence of geological variation
A possible difference in geographical origin, requiring contextual interpretation
feedback: Stable isotope comparisons are not automatically numerical clocks.
Isotope ratios do not preserve language.
Geological variation is one reason baselines matter.
Correct. Mobility interpretation depends on environmental and biological context.
questions.explanation: Correct. Mobility interpretation depends on environmental and biological context.

questions.prompt: Explain why an age for volcanic ash and an age for associated fossil bone need not describe the same event.
questions.model: Volcanic minerals can record formation or cooling of an eruption-related deposit. Bone may record a biological event or acquire later chemical changes, depending on the method. Sediment containing the fossil can have another depositional history. Stratigraphy and taphonomy must establish how these events relate. Secure associated layers can constrain fossil context, but their ages should not simply be relabelled as direct fossil measurements.
criteria: Identify different dated materials or events.
Explain the role of stratigraphy and association.
Avoid treating an associated-layer age as automatically direct.

questions.prompt: A student uses a stable carbon isotope result as a fossil’s numerical age. Correct the interpretation and describe a better age strategy.
questions.model: Stable carbon isotope ratios can contribute to dietary or environmental interpretation when suitable baselines are available; they do not by themselves provide elapsed time in years. An age strategy should first identify the sample material and its context, then select a suitable chronological method such as radiocarbon for appropriate recent organic material or volcanic-mineral dating for older associated layers. Independent stratigraphic checks strengthen the conclusion.
criteria: Distinguish a proxy from a chronological clock.
Select a method matched to material and likely age.
Include contextual or independent checking.

summary: Identify what material and event a date represents.
Relative ordering and numerical methods answer different but complementary questions.
Radioactive fractions decline exponentially by repeated halving.
Stable-isotope and climate evidence can provide context without directly dating a fossil.
sourceNotes: Scope adapted from Surfing WACE Human Biology Unit 4 (2017); explanations, models and questions are original.
Dating overview: https://humanorigins.si.edu/evidence/dating
Radiocarbon is described as sample-dependent, around 50 ka, not a guaranteed 70 ka range. Fluorine is not treated as a universal numerical clock.

title: Models for Human Evolutionary Trees
objectives: Interpret branching as common ancestry rather than progress.
Compare anatomical, nuclear, mitochondrial and Y-linked evidence.
Explain why sampling and gene flow can require model revision.

glossary.definition: An ancestor and all its descendants.
A branching history inferred for a particular genetic region.
A model of the branching history of populations or species.

slides.title: A tree is a relationship model
slides.html: An evolutionary tree proposes patterns of shared ancestry. A branching point represents a common ancestral population, not necessarily a named fossil specimen. The order of branch connections matters; the position of a tip on the left or right does not rank species by intelligence or worth. Several related lineages can exist at the same time.

slides.title: Fossils test proposed branches
slides.html: Researchers compare anatomical characters, geographical context and reliable ages. A fossil may combine ancestral and derived traits, making placement uncertain. Absence from an incomplete fossil record is not evidence that a population never existed. Proposed direct ancestry requires more support than an older date and one feature resembling a later species.

slides.title: Measurement and imaging
slides.html: Measurements help compare size and shape, while CT imaging can reveal internal structures without cutting through an entire fossil. Surface microscopy can investigate wear or marks. Each technique addresses a defined question and has limits, including distortion and reconstruction choices. Digital visualisation does not eliminate uncertainty or turn an incomplete specimen into a complete original.

slides.title: Nuclear DNA samples many histories
slides.html: Nuclear DNA is inherited from both parents and is reshuffled by recombination. Comparisons across many regions can inform population divergence, relatedness and admixture. However, different regions may retain different histories. Preservation and modern contamination are major issues in ancient DNA, and conclusions should consider the amount and quality of recovered sequence rather than only its age.

slides.title: Mitochondrial and Y-linked lineages
slides.html: Mitochondrial DNA usually tracks a maternal line, while suitable non-recombining Y-chromosome regions track a paternal line in people carrying a Y chromosome. These are informative but narrow genealogical routes, not the whole ancestry of a population. The relevant evidence is DNA sequence variation; a Y chromosome is not itself an amino acid sequence.

slides.title: A common ancestor is not the only ancestor
slides.html: The most recent common maternal ancestor of sampled mitochondrial lineages was not the only woman alive at that time, nor the sole ancestor of all human genes. Other individuals can contribute ancestry through different routes. Genealogical lineages can disappear through chance even when descendants persist through other branches of the family network.

slides.title: Branching and admixture
slides.html: A simple tree can show that two groups share a more recent ancestor with each other than with an outgroup. Historical interbreeding adds connections that a tree alone does not display. Human evolutionary models therefore may need both branching relationships and gene-flow information. Neither genetic mixing nor incomplete lineage sorting should be confused with a ladder of progress.

diagram.caption: A simplified branching relationship. Gene flow between these and other populations requires additional evidence and connections.

slides.title: Why models change
slides.html: New fossils, revised dates and improved genetic sampling can support or weaken particular branch placements. Scientific revision does not mean that every previous observation was false. It means that the explanatory model is being tested against a wider evidence base. State which connection changed and what new information justified the change, rather than saying the whole evolutionary history was reset.

diagram.caption: Evidence streams constrain a model together. The sequence is a simplified workflow, not a guarantee that every fossil preserves DNA.

questions.prompt: What does the left-to-right order of tips on a tree establish?
options: A fixed intelligence ranking
Nothing by itself about evolutionary superiority; branch connections determine relationships
The exact age of every fossil
That the rightmost species is everyone’s ancestor
feedback: Trees do not rank intelligence.
Correct. Rotating a branch can change tip positions without changing ancestry.
Ages need an explicit scale or dated evidence.
A tip is not automatically the ancestor of another tip.
questions.explanation: Correct. Rotating a branch can change tip positions without changing ancestry.

questions.prompt: Why is mitochondrial DNA not a complete record of human ancestry?
options: It contains no variation.
It is inherited from every ancestor equally.
It represents one maternal lineage rather than all nuclear genealogies.
It is made of amino acids rather than DNA.
feedback: Mitochondrial sequence variation is informative.
It tracks a restricted inheritance route.
Correct. Whole ancestry involves many other genealogical contributions.
Mitochondrial DNA is a nucleic acid.
questions.explanation: Correct. Whole ancestry involves many other genealogical contributions.

questions.prompt: Which finding could justify revising a fossil’s placement?
options: A securely dated specimen with previously unknown diagnostic anatomy
A desire to make a perfectly straight ladder
A new colour chosen for a diagram
The rule that old fossils cannot have derived traits
feedback: Correct. New evidence can alter the best-supported relationship model.
A preferred visual shape is not evidence.
Display colour does not change relationships.
Fossils can show mosaics of traits.
questions.explanation: Correct. New evidence can alter the best-supported relationship model.

questions.prompt: Why may a human history model need more than a branching tree?
options: Trees can never represent common ancestry.
All genes always have identical histories.
Recombination makes every fossil younger.
Historical gene flow connects diverged populations.
feedback: Common ancestry is precisely what branching trees represent.
Genomic regions may have differing histories.
Recombination does not directly change geological fossil age.
Correct. Admixture adds connections beyond simple bifurcation.
questions.explanation: Correct. Admixture adds connections beyond simple bifurcation.

questions.prompt: Correct the statement: mitochondrial Eve was the only woman alive and supplied every gene in all living humans.
questions.model: The label refers to a common ancestor of particular surviving maternal mitochondrial lineages, not the only woman of her time. Other women and men can contribute to nuclear ancestry through different genealogical paths. Some maternal lines cease to be represented without eliminating all descendants. Consequently, a mitochondrial common ancestor is a locus-specific genealogical inference, not a claim of a one-woman population or sole origin of every gene.
criteria: Explain the restricted maternal inheritance route.
Distinguish a surviving lineage from the whole population.
Recognise contributions to nuclear ancestry from other people.

questions.prompt: Explain how an anatomical tree and a genetic dataset can be compared without assuming either is automatically perfect.
questions.model: An anatomical tree groups fossils using measured characters and assumptions about their evolution, while genetic comparisons use inherited sequence variation and particular evolutionary models. Both depend on sampling and can be affected by missing information. Agreement strengthens a relationship hypothesis; disagreement can prompt checks for convergence, preservation, gene flow or differing gene histories. The response should identify testable explanations rather than dismiss one evidence type by default.
criteria: Describe the different evidence bases.
Identify sampling or model limitations.
Explain how agreement or disagreement informs testing.

summary: Trees represent common ancestry, not a ranking of species.
Different genetic regions can have different genealogical histories.
Maternal or paternal lineage markers do not represent all ancestry.
New evidence and gene flow can require more complex models.
sourceNotes: Scope adapted from Surfing WACE Human Biology Unit 4 (2017); explanations, models and questions are original.
Molecular evidence and admixture context: https://humanorigins.si.edu/evidence/genetics/ancient-dna-and-neanderthals
Corrected the source’s description of Y-chromosome evidence: relevant comparisons concern DNA sequences, not “amino acid sequences on the chromosome”.

title: Models for Evolution of Homo sapiens
objectives: Compare classical regional continuity and replacement models.
Explain why African origins and admixture can both be supported.
Evaluate fossil and genetic evidence without racial ladder interpretations.

glossary.definition: A historical model proposing long-term regional evolution linked by gene flow.
A model emphasising dispersal of modern humans and replacement of earlier groups.
Genetic mixing between previously differentiated populations.

slides.title: Models address related questions
slides.html: Models of modern-human origins explain where the lineage emerged, how populations dispersed and how much contact occurred with other hominins. These are distinguishable questions. An African origin does not, by definition, settle every later migration date or require that dispersing populations never interbred. Evaluate each claim against the type of evidence that can test it.

slides.title: Classical regional continuity
slides.html: The classical multiregional model proposed that geographically spread earlier Homo populations contributed through continuing regional evolution and gene flow to later modern humans. Gene flow was essential to the model’s account of a connected species. It should not be misrepresented as completely independent origins of different living human species in separate continents.

slides.title: A strict replacement version
slides.html: A strict recent-African-replacement model emphasised the origin of modern humans in Africa followed by dispersal that replaced other populations with little or no interbreeding. It generated testable expectations about dates, fossil distributions and genetic ancestry. The strongest zero-interbreeding version is not supported by later nuclear evidence showing contributions from Neanderthals and Denisovans.

slides.title: Evidence for African origins
slides.html: Early fossils attributed to Homo sapiens occur in Africa, and genetic patterns support a deep African history. Greater diversity in a population can be consistent with a longer history, but diversity also depends on population size, structure, migration and sampling. No single mitochondrial observation alone specifies every place and date involved in the emergence of the species.

slides.title: Admixture refines the model
slides.html: Ancient-genome comparisons demonstrate contact between modern humans and other lineages. The resulting account combines predominantly African origins with later dispersal and some admixture. This is not equivalent to proving every prediction of classical multiregionalism, nor does it erase evidence for African origins. Scientific models can retain supported components while changing others.

diagram.caption: Simplified divergence relationships. Interbreeding is a further feature of the history and cannot be inferred merely from the tree’s tip order.

slides.title: Different genomes, different records
slides.html: Mitochondrial DNA, non-recombining Y regions and nuclear loci follow different inheritance paths. A lineage absent from present-day mitochondrial samples may still have contributed nuclear DNA through interbreeding. Modern distributions were also affected by later movements. A genetic result therefore needs a clearly stated inheritance model rather than an assumption that every locus reports the same single history.

slides.title: Migration maps are models
slides.html: An arrow on a map summarises a proposed movement; it is not a direct observation of every journey. Fossil sites, dated artefacts, environmental barriers and genomic signals constrain possible routes. Several dispersals and returns can occur. Lower sea levels altered some coastlines and connections, but did not remove every water barrier or make all regions accessible by land.

slides.title: What a good comparison concludes
slides.html: A strong account separates classical model predictions from current evidence. It recognises African origins, population structure and later contact without describing living groups as more primitive or more evolved. Human variation is not a set of separate evolutionary ladders. Remaining uncertainties concern particular populations, dates and routes, not whether all living humans share substantial common ancestry.

diagram.caption: A qualitative history model. Stages overlap and contain multiple episodes; this is not a dated or exclusive migration route.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly relates African origins to later admixture?
options: They are logically incompatible.
They concern distinguishable events and can both be supported.
Admixture requires every modern population to be a different species.
African origins prove no population ever migrated back.
feedback: Origin and later genetic exchange can both occur.
Correct. A lineage may originate in Africa and interbreed after dispersal.
Admixture does not require separate living species.
Return migration is a separate empirical question.
questions.explanation: Correct. A lineage may originate in Africa and interbreed after dispersal.

questions.prompt: Which prediction of a strict zero-admixture replacement model is challenged by ancient nuclear DNA?
options: That all humans share ancestry
That fossils have geographical locations
That dispersing modern humans made no genetic contribution exchanges with other lineages
That mutation occurs
feedback: Shared ancestry is not the challenged claim here.
Genetics does not remove fossil geography.
Correct. Introgressed nuclear segments document historical interbreeding.
The existence of mutation is not what this model comparison tests.
questions.explanation: Correct. Introgressed nuclear segments document historical interbreeding.

questions.prompt: Why can one mitochondrial lineage fail to reveal all ancient contact?
options: It samples a restricted maternal history rather than the entire recombining genome.
Every mitochondrial sample contains every ancestor’s DNA.
Mitochondria prevent all interbreeding.
A single locus directly maps every migration route.
feedback: Correct. Other ancestral contributions can persist elsewhere in the genome.
This confuses a restricted lineage with total ancestry.
An organelle does not make all population contact impossible.
One locus cannot specify every route without further evidence.
questions.explanation: Correct. Other ancestral contributions can persist elsewhere in the genome.

questions.prompt: How should arrows on an ancient migration map be interpreted?
options: As exact recordings of every individual journey
As evidence that oceans never formed barriers
As rankings of modern populations
As summaries of hypotheses constrained by sites, dates and other evidence
feedback: Ancient journeys are inferred rather than all directly recorded.
Water barriers remained important in many regions.
Migration maps should not rank people.
Correct. Map models compress evidence and uncertainty.
questions.explanation: Correct. Map models compress evidence and uncertainty.

questions.prompt: Compare a strict replacement model with an African-origin model that includes admixture.
questions.model: Both accounts can place the emergence of Homo sapiens in Africa and include later dispersal. A strict replacement version expects little or no genetic contribution from displaced lineages. An admixture account allows interbreeding and inherited Neanderthal or Denisovan contributions while retaining African origins. Ancient nuclear genomes challenge the zero-interbreeding expectation, so the distinction concerns population interaction rather than a choice between African origins and all gene flow.
criteria: Identify the shared African-origin/dispersal component.
Contrast expectations about interbreeding.
Link the model refinement to nuclear genetic evidence.

questions.prompt: Explain why greater genetic diversity in Africa supports an origin argument but does not alone reconstruct every migration.
questions.model: Greater diversity can reflect a longer population history, making it relevant to African-origin models. However, diversity is also affected by population size, structure, drift, admixture and sampling. A single pattern does not specify all dispersal dates or routes. Fossil ages, archaeological context and many genetic regions must be combined, with explicit models, to infer a more detailed population history.
criteria: Connect diversity to a possible longer history.
Identify other processes affecting diversity.
Explain the need for multiple independent evidence streams.

summary: Classical models make distinct predictions about continuity, dispersal and replacement.
African origins can coexist with later admixture.
Nuclear genomes add evidence not captured by one maternal lineage.
Current models are branching population histories, not racial progress ladders.
sourceNotes: Scope adapted from Surfing WACE Human Biology Unit 4 (2017); explanations, models and questions are original.
Current gene-flow context: https://humanorigins.si.edu/evidence/genetics/ancient-dna-and-neanderthals
Fossil-origin context: https://humanorigins.si.edu/evidence/human-fossils/species/homo-sapiens
Historical claims about Mungo mtDNA and strict no-admixture replacement are not repeated as established conclusions.

title: Development of Culture
objectives: Distinguish cultural transmission from genetic inheritance.
Interpret changes in tools, subsistence and settlement through evidence.
Explain feedbacks between cultural practices, population and environment.

glossary.definition: Learned and socially transmitted practices, knowledge and meanings.
An implement made from components or materials combined together.
Retention and modification of socially transmitted knowledge across generations.

slides.title: Culture is socially transmitted
slides.html: Culture includes learned techniques, knowledge, communication and shared practices. Transmission can occur between relatives, unrelated people and neighbouring groups. A new practice can spread within a lifetime without a corresponding new mutation. Biological capacities make learning possible, but a particular tool design or custom should not be treated as an allele inherited in a simple Mendelian pattern.

slides.title: Tools preserve only part of culture
slides.html: Stone tools survive more readily than many wooden, plant-fibre or spoken traditions. The archaeological record therefore samples past behaviour unevenly. A lack of preserved artefacts does not establish a complete absence of culture. Researchers compare manufacture, use-wear, residues and context to infer activities while recognising that much learned behaviour may leave little durable trace.

slides.title: Technological change is not a ladder
slides.html: Core tools, flakes, bifacial handaxes and blades reflect different manufacturing choices and uses. Their broad historical ordering is useful, but forms overlap in time and vary regionally. Later people can use simple tools effectively, and similar techniques can occur in different populations. Do not rank the worth or intelligence of peoples solely by one tool category.

diagram.caption: Schematic technological forms, not an inevitable sequence followed by every population. Different forms can coexist and serve different tasks.

slides.title: Planning and composite manufacture
slides.html: Prepared-core techniques shape a core before a planned flake is removed. Composite tools combine parts, such as a stone point attached to a shaft, and may require adhesives or bindings. These processes can support inferences about skill and knowledge transmission. They do not directly reveal the exact language used to teach a technique or all the makers’ social relationships.

slides.title: Symbols and social information
slides.html: Ornaments, art, pigments and patterned object use may carry meanings shared within a group. Secure context and alternative practical functions must be considered before interpreting them symbolically. The occurrence of a symbol-like artefact can inform an argument about communication, but its particular meaning may remain unknown. Cultural evidence differs from a complete written account of past beliefs.

slides.title: Agriculture and settlement
slides.html: Food production developed in different places and at different times rather than through one simultaneous worldwide revolution. Cultivation and domestication could support denser, more permanent settlements and new labour roles. They also changed diets, workloads, disease environments and ecological pressures. These outcomes were variable; agriculture was not automatically an immediate improvement in every individual’s health or food security.

slides.title: Technology and demographic change
slides.html: Metallurgy, transport and industrial production altered the resources people could obtain and the environments they created. Sanitation, public-health measures and medical knowledge also changed survival patterns. Population growth reflects births, deaths and migration rather than one invention alone. Explain the mechanisms and timing instead of assigning a complex demographic change to a single famous inventor.

slides.title: Culture and genes can interact
slides.html: A cultural practice can change the environment in which natural selection acts. For example, sustained use of particular foods can create conditions that favour inherited physiological variants in some populations. The learned practice and the genetic variant remain different things. This reciprocal relationship is called gene–culture coevolution; it does not mean every cultural difference has a direct genetic cause.

diagram.caption: A qualitative gene–culture feedback model. Cultural transmission and genetic inheritance are distinct, and effects depend on context.

slides.title: Evaluate cultural claims with context
slides.html: To compare cultures archaeologically, specify the evidence, its age, preservation and possible functions. Associations between species and industries are not exclusive identity rules. Likewise, more permanent settlement does not measure a society’s human value. An evidence-based account recognises diverse successful ways of living, uneven preservation and the continuing interaction of learning, ecology and population history.

questions.prompt: Which example is cultural transmission?
options: A child inherits a chromosome through a gamete.
A DNA base changes during replication.
A learner acquires a knapping technique from an unrelated expert.
An isotope undergoes radioactive decay.
feedback: This is biological inheritance.
This is a mutation process, not social learning.
Correct. Learned knowledge can pass between unrelated people.
Radioactive decay is not cultural learning.
questions.explanation: Correct. Learned knowledge can pass between unrelated people.

questions.prompt: Why does the archaeological record underrepresent some past practices?
options: Organic materials and spoken knowledge often preserve poorly.
All useful objects are made of stone.
Absence of a surviving tool proves no learning occurred.
Every past action leaves an equally durable object.
feedback: Correct. Preservation biases affect what survives to be studied.
Many important technologies use less durable materials.
Preservation and sampling must be considered.
Actions differ greatly in their material traces.
questions.explanation: Correct. Preservation biases affect what survives to be studied.

questions.prompt: What is a composite tool?
options: A tool that must contain a new allele
A tool belonging to exactly one hominin species
An unmodified rock with no possible use
An implement made by combining components or materials
feedback: A learned design is not an allele.
Tool design is not automatically an exclusive species marker.
The term refers to construction, not lack of modification.
Correct. A hafted point and shaft provide a familiar example.
questions.explanation: Correct. A hafted point and shaft provide a familiar example.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes gene–culture coevolution?
options: Every cultural difference is genetically fixed.
Learned practices can alter selection pressures, while inherited biology can affect those practices.
Cultural information can be transmitted only through gametes.
Agriculture began everywhere at one exact date.
feedback: This is an unjustified genetic explanation of all culture.
Correct. The interaction retains a distinction between learning and genetic inheritance.
Culture can spread by social learning.
Agricultural histories were regionally varied.
questions.explanation: Correct. The interaction retains a distinction between learning and genetic inheritance.

questions.prompt: Explain why a sequence of core tools, handaxes and blades should not be used as a simple intelligence ranking of human populations.
questions.model: Tool forms reflect manufacture, function, resources and learned traditions as well as chronology. Different forms can overlap and remain effective for particular tasks. Preservation also makes some technologies more visible than others. Therefore, one artefact category cannot provide a direct universal scale of intelligence or human value. A justified comparison examines context, technical requirements and evidence for knowledge transmission rather than imposing a cultural ladder.
criteria: Explain functional and regional variation.
Recognise overlap or preservation bias.
Reject a direct universal intelligence or worth ranking.

questions.prompt: Describe two ways that increasing settlement density could change population biology, without assuming all effects are beneficial.
questions.model: More permanent food production can support a larger population and specialised labour, but denser settlement may also increase exposure to infectious agents and waste. Diets and workloads can change, sometimes creating nutritional or health problems. These altered conditions may affect birth and death rates and the selection pressures experienced by inherited variants. The effects depend on environment, social arrangements and technology rather than following one universally beneficial sequence.
criteria: Link settlement or food production to a demographic mechanism.
Explain a possible cost or health pressure.
Distinguish contextual outcomes from inevitable progress.

summary: Culture is learned and can spread between unrelated individuals.
Preservation biases limit archaeological reconstructions.
Technologies overlap and cannot rank human worth or intelligence.
Food production, settlement and industrialisation changed environments and demography.
Gene–culture coevolution connects, but does not equate, learning and inheritance.
sourceNotes: Scope adapted from Surfing WACE Human Biology Unit 4 (2017); explanations, models and questions are original.
The source’s universal progress ladder and single-date worldwide revolutions are replaced with regionally variable, evidence-limited interpretations.
Tool attribution is not treated as exclusive to one species; cultural and biological processes remain distinguished.
